payload.request:
Add a delete endpoint to the existing URL shortener.

DELETE /api/v1/links/{code} removes a link and its click statistics. It returns 204 with no
body on success, and 404 when no link with that code exists. A deleted code must behave
exactly as an unknown one afterwards: GET /{code} returns 404, and the stats endpoint
returns 404.

Deleting is permanent; there is no soft delete and no recovery. Keep the existing behaviour
of every other endpoint unchanged.

payload.question: What authentication/authorization should DELETE /api/v1/links/{code} require, given the request specifies none explicitly?

options.name: Reuse existing endpoint auth pattern
options.summary: Apply whatever authentication/authorization middleware the existing endpoints (e.g. link creation) already use, unchanged, to the new DELETE route.

options.name: No authentication (public delete)
options.summary: Allow any caller who knows a code to delete it, with no access check.
options.rejectedBecause: A destructive, irreversible operation with no access control is a plausible but risky default; if the existing system has any auth on write endpoints, silently omitting it here would be a real security regression, not a minor detail.

options.name: New elevated/admin-only permission
options.summary: Introduce a stricter permission tier specifically for deletion, separate from what other endpoints use.
options.rejectedBecause: Not requested anywhere in the text, and inventing a new authorization tier would expand scope beyond 'add a delete endpoint' without any signal that one is needed.

payload.rationale: This is a brownfield task with existing code available; the convention already in use by other write endpoints is discoverable by inspection rather than requiring a guess about intent, and 'keep the existing behaviour of every other endpoint unchanged' signals consistency with current conventions is expected.

payload.value: Add a permanent DELETE endpoint (DELETE /api/v1/links/{code}) to the existing URL shortener that removes a link and its click statistics, returns 204 on success and 404 when the code is unknown, and leaves every other endpoint's behaviour unchanged.

payload.question: How should LinkRepository detect and perform the removal of a link and its click statistics for DELETE /api/v1/links/{code}, given both live in one row of one table?

options.name: Single DELETE statement, affected-row count as the existence signal
options.summary: One `DELETE FROM links WHERE code = $code` via ExecuteNonQueryAsync; 0 rows affected means the code never existed (or was already deleted), 1 means it did and is now gone.

options.name: SELECT existence check, then DELETE
options.summary: Query for the row first, return 404 if absent, otherwise issue a separate DELETE.
options.rejectedBecause: Reintroduces the exact time-of-check-to-time-of-use race ADR 0001 already rejected for alias creation; a concurrent delete or recreate between the two statements can make the check stale, and it doubles round-trips on a path the NFRs require to match other single-record writes' latency.

options.name: DELETE ... RETURNING code (mirroring RedirectAsync's pattern)
options.summary: Use SQLite's RETURNING clause and check whether the reader produced a row.
options.rejectedBecause: RedirectAsync needs RETURNING because it must hand original_url back to the caller; delete has no data to return, only an existence fact, so RETURNING plus a reader is strictly more code and a reader to open/dispose for no benefit over a plain affected-row count.

options.name: Soft delete / tombstone row
options.summary: Mark the row deleted (flag or nulled fields) instead of removing it, to allow future recovery or auditing.
options.rejectedBecause: The requirement and its AC8/NFR explicitly forbid any recoverable or hidden state after deletion; any retained row, flagged or not, violates that outright.

payload.chosen: Single DELETE statement, affected-row count as the existence signal
payload.rationale: The data model already puts a link and its click count in one row (no separate stats table), so a single DML statement is already atomic for both AC2/AC3/AC10 at once; using its own affected-row count to disambiguate found/not-found needs no extra read, matches the no-TOCTOU precedent ADR 0001 established for create, and gives idempotency (AC9) and the identical-404 requirement (AC7) for free.

payload.question: What type should carry the result of a delete attempt from LinkRepository through LinkService to the HTTP layer?

options.name: Plain bool ("a row existed and was removed")
options.summary: DeleteAsync returns Task<bool>; Program.cs maps true to 204 and false to 404.

options.name: A new discriminated result type, e.g. DeleteOutcome { Deleted, NotFound }, matching the CreateOutcome/RedirectResult convention
options.summary: Add a dedicated enum-backed class for symmetry with the two existing multi-outcome result types.
options.rejectedBecause: CreateOutcome and RedirectResult carry outcome-specific data (a code/URL, or an error message) alongside the discriminator; delete has exactly two outcomes and neither carries any payload, so a dedicated type would only wrap a bool in ceremony the codebase's own convention doesn't require — those types exist to carry data, not for discrimination's own sake.

payload.chosen: Plain bool ("a row existed and was removed")
payload.rationale: Keeps the addition proportional to what it does: a binary fact with no associated payload doesn't need a discriminated type to be introduced into Models.cs; introducing one would be complexity spent on a distinction (naming outcomes) that a bool already conveys unambiguously at the two call sites that consume it.

payload.question: Should delete tests be in separate files or merged with existing test files?

options.name: Separate files per component
options.summary: Create LinkRepositoryDeleteTests.cs and LinkServiceDeleteTests.cs to keep delete-specific tests isolated and make test discovery/reading clearer

options.name: Append to existing files
options.summary: Add delete tests to the existing LinkRepositoryTests.cs and LinkServiceTests.cs alongside other tests
options.rejectedBecause: The existing test files are already 200+ lines each; separating delete tests keeps concerns distinct and makes the test file size manageable for future maintenance. The separate-files pattern also mirrors how the tests discovered the implementation was already written (separate methods in repository and service), making the test organization naturally follow the code organization.

payload.rationale: The implementation split delete into its own methods (DeleteAsync in both LinkRepository and LinkService), so the tests follow that shape. Separate files keep the test organization isomorphic with the implementation, make the suites easier to scan, and avoid pushing existing test files past 250 lines.

payload.question: How to fix xUnit analyzer warnings about Assert.True for substrings and Assert.NotNull on value types?

options.name: Use Assert.StartsWith, Assert.Null/Assert.NotNull appropriately
options.summary: Replace Assert.True(s.Contains(...)) with Assert.Contains(...), remove Assert.NotNull on DateTimeOffset, use targeted assertions per xUnit2009/xUnit2002 rules

options.name: Suppress warnings
options.summary: Add #pragma directives to silence xUnit2009 and xUnit2002 without changing the assertions
options.rejectedBecause: The warnings identify genuinely better patterns (Assert.Contains/Assert.StartsWith are more readable and provide better failure messages than Assert.True(Contains(...))); silencing them hides real opportunities for test quality.

payload.rationale: The warnings are correct; xUnit's specialized assertions (Assert.StartsWith, Assert.Contains) produce clearer failure messages and are the documented best practice. The fix eliminates technical debt and improves test readability at no cost.

payload.question: What should the delete test suite exercise, given that 82% coverage is the measured figure?

options.name: Comprehensive delete coverage (all code paths and side effects)
options.summary: Test delete with and without the code existing, deletion twice, post-deletion GET/stats, code reuse after delete, interaction with click counts, and expiry state—basically, every branch delete touches

options.name: Minimal happy-path only
options.summary: Test delete success and delete 404 only, leaving the rest (post-deletion behavior, double-delete, reuse) uncovered
options.rejectedBecause: The previous test run left these behaviors untested; they are the high-value cases the requirement explicitly calls for (AC5, AC6, AC9). A minimal suite would not justify the measured 0.82 coverage or defend against the specific regressions in the impact analysis (§2, §5 of docs/impact-analysis.md).

payload.chosen: Comprehensive delete coverage (all code paths and side effects)
payload.rationale: The requirement calls for delete to be observable through other endpoints' behavior (AC5, AC6, AC9, AC11 regression). Tests that only verify delete's own 204/404 response would miss silent regressions where delete silently affects the wrong rows (impact analysis §5). The measured 0.82 coverage figure reflects testing the full interaction surface: delete itself, the immediately-visible side effects (post-delete stats/redirect/double-delete), and the critical invariant (code reuse after delete).
